dossiers.title: Major ICT incident reporting
dossiers.kicker: From event boundary to reporting channel
dossiers.summary: DORA incident classification, economic-impact inputs and reporting requirements, linked to the controlling provisions and relevant EBA Final Q&A.
dossiers.audience: Operational resilience, incident response and regulatory reporting teams

sections.title: Incident boundary: impact on financial-entity services
sections.body: A phishing attack confined to a customer's private sphere is not, by itself, an ICT-related incident of the financial entity. The assessment changes when the entity is targeted and the event compromises its network and information systems in a way that adversely affects service availability, authenticity, integrity or confidentiality. Classification thresholds still have to be tested before major-incident reporting follows.

sections.title: Major-incident criteria and materiality thresholds
sections.body: After an event meets the ICT-related incident boundary, it still has to be classified under DORA Article 18. The incident-classification RTS specifies how major incidents and their materiality thresholds are determined; reaching the event boundary alone does not complete that assessment.

sections.title: Economic impact: incident work and preventive training
sections.body: For the economic-impact assessment, staff costs can include overtime and the time staff allocate to managing the incident. Preventive training costs are outside that incident-cost calculation. The official answer does not prescribe one calculation method, so the entity should retain a consistent and explainable method for its estimate.

sections.title: Reporting route for significant institutions
sections.body: For significant institutions, incidents that qualify as major under DORA are classified and reported under DORA and its related standards. The EBA answer says this avoids duplicate reporting through the earlier ECB SSM cyber-incident framework.

dossiers.title: ICT third-party service scope
dossiers.kicker: Classify the service before mapping the chain
dossiers.summary: The DORA ICT-service definition, non-ICT service chains and critical-function reassessment, with the relevant legal and EBA Q&A evidence.
dossiers.audience: Third-party risk, procurement, outsourcing and register owners

sections.title: Statutory ICT-service definition
sections.body: A provider's label does not settle the classification. Payment-processing or infrastructure services can be ICT services when they satisfy DORA Article 3(21), but this does not make every service supplied by that provider an ICT service. The official answer identifies services without a prevailing ICT component, including certain clearing and settlement activities, as a boundary that requires attention.

sections.title: Non-ICT provider chains
sections.body: The EBA answer states that an ICT subcontractor of a non-ICT service provider is normally outside the register of information. The presence of technology somewhere in the supply chain does not, by itself, turn the direct service into an ICT service for register purposes.

sections.title: Critical-function reassessment
sections.body: The default result can change when the financial entity's assessment shows that the subcontracted ICT service is effectively equivalent to direct ICT support for a critical or important function. Record the supplied function and the reasoning used to include or exclude the contractual chain; a vendor-category label is not enough.

dossiers.title: Register of information
dossiers.summary: Article 28 register duties, consolidated scope and source-dated submission requirements, linked to the register ITS and EBA Final Q&A.
dossiers.audience: Register owners, data governance, third-party risk and reporting teams

sections.title: Register duty under the simplified framework
sections.body: Entities using the Article 16 simplified ICT risk-management framework still maintain the register required by Article 28. Proportionality may affect the complexity of implementation, but the EBA answer does not treat it as an exemption from the obligation.

sections.title: Annual communication and annual submission
sections.body: The annual register submission generally fulfils the annual communication in Article 28(3), so a second duplicate annual report is not required.

sections.title: Competent-authority access on request
sections.body: Article 28(3) requires financial entities to make the full register of information, or requested sections of it, available to the competent authority upon request. The annual submission does not replace this separate access duty.

sections.title: Planned critical arrangements
sections.body: The annual submission also does not replace the duty to inform the competent authority in a timely manner about planned contractual arrangements for ICT services supporting critical or important functions, or when an existing function becomes critical or important.

sections.title: Consolidated register perimeter
sections.body: For a register maintained at consolidated or sub-consolidated level, the official answer links the reporting perimeter to the entities and branches included in the applicable consolidation scope, rather than drawing a simple EU-versus-non-EU subsidiary line.

sections.title: Reference periods and template codes
sections.body: For the 2025 exercise, the official answer sets the reference period to 31 March 2025; from 2026 onward it is 31 December of the preceding year. A separate answer corrects the B_06.01 template numbering and points reporters to the codes in the reporting package. These operational values should be checked against the current official package for each submission cycle.

timeSensitivity.note: Reference periods, template numbering and reporting-package codes are source-dated. Recheck the current official package before each submission cycle.
